clue.text: (13ac.) US gun lobby pushes its own interpretation of this support net, working with mad men

definitions.text: US gun lobby pushes its own interpretation of this

parts.note: to support a motion formally is to back it, the same word as the one after first

indicators.note: letters that are working are set in motion and moved about, so they end up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A satirical swipe at the American gun lobby and its self-serving reading of the constitution, with a nod to the TV series Mad Men.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across two lights, 1 and 13 across. 'Mad Men' looks like the TV drama and 'working' like a job, but the drama title is just fodder for the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Second Amendment to the US Constitution concerns the right to bear arms, which the National Rifle Association reads very broadly.

clue.text: Hanging state has American president in sight, perhaps

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it

parts.note: sight is one example of the five senses, hence 'perhaps'
US is the standard short form for American
P is a common abbreviation for president

explanation.surface: A hung election result leaves the country waiting to see which American president takes office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American president' reads as one person but splits into two abbreviations, US and P, which go together inside the word for sight and its kin.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspense is a condition of being left undecided and waiting, a figurative kind of dangling or hanging in the air.

clue.text: Maybe King Brian's entourage amounts to sod all in short

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, surrounded on both sides

parts.note: a curt reply is a short one
sod all is slang for nothing, and nothing is the letter O

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict that a would-be king's hangers-on are worth nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sod all' is British slang for nothing at all, which in crosswords is the round letter O; 'in short' looks like 'briefly' but is really the zero going inside the word for brusque.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's court is the body of courtiers and attendants surrounding a ruler, so it is a royal retinue; 'Maybe' flags the king as one example.

clue.text: Republican sneak dipped into Green's account

indicators.note: something dipped into a liquid ends up inside it, surrounded

parts.note: green means inexperienced or naive
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican
a rat is a sneak or informer

explanation.surface: A political scandal: a Republican snoop has been poking around in a Green politician's finances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' has a capital so it looks like a party or a surname, and 'account' looks like a bank account; green here means callow, and the account is a story.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative is a spoken or written telling of events, which is one common sense of an account.

clue.text: Press gets independent state mocking

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: The newspapers turn to ridicule an independent-minded state or nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like the media, but it is the verb for smoothing clothes. CAL for California is a crossword staple for 'state'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironical is a less common form of ironic, describing words that say one thing while meaning the scornful opposite.

clue.text: Apparently Hancock doesn't have them, right, with waders

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
egrets are long-legged wading birds of the heron family

explanation.surface: A jab at Matt Hancock, the disgraced former UK health secretary, apparently unrepentant, pictured alongside someone in fishing boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waders' suggests rubber fishing boots but means birds that wade. Hancock, UK health secretary during Covid, was widely seen as unapologetic about his conduct.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is a topical description: things someone feels sorry about, which the politician apparently lacks, in the sense of 'no apologies'.

clue.text: Called in Braverman (a meddler)

indicators.note: the letters sought lie in the following words, running across their word breaks

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the surname through 'a' into the start of the last word

explanation.surface: Suella Braverman, the former UK home secretary, gets called in and labelled a meddler.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts with the last two letters of Braverman, takes the whole of 'a', and ends with the first three letters of meddler; the brackets are only there for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To be called something is to be given that title or label, so the past participles match.

clue.text: Money went out round university for possible snack item

parts.note: cash is money

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it on every side
something put out of place or out of order is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'Went out' reads as spending, but 'out' shuffles the four letters, and the rearranged letters then wrap around the university letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashew nuts are commonly eaten salted or roasted as a bar snack, so they are one example of a nibble; 'possible' flags the example.

clue.text: Place ball and chain (just the top) in behind

indicators.note: things put in something else are enclosed by it

a ball is round, like the letter O

explanation.definitionFit: To place something is to find where it is or to position it, both senses shared with the verb in the grid.

clue.text: Finished with engagement? Change to a later model

explanation.definitionFit: To update is to bring something up to date, replacing an old version with the newest one available.

clue.text: Once uncool, Margaret's not one to fit in?

parts.note: square is dated slang for uncool, hence 'once'

explanation.surface: A woman called Margaret, formerly unfashionable, never quite belonged.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Margaret joins the wordplay to the definition, standing for 'is'. The question mark admits the definition is an idiom rather than a dictionary synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A square peg in a round hole is the proverbial misfit, a person unsuited to their surroundings or role.

clue.text: More from one-time model getting arse reduced

explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, in excess of the usual amount, which is what more means as an adjective.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Persist in hiding little Ms Westwood in safe

indicators.note: whatever is hiding something keeps it tucked away inside

parts.note: safe and sure both mean certain or reliable
Vivienne Westwood, the British fashion designer, shortened to her nickname

clue.text: Allude to arbiter shafted by the state

clue.text: Swear, etc about result

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
